proxy_input: How does 1080 stadia use so much more data than 1080 video/youtube.
target_output:
“1080p” only describes the **resolution** (1920×1080). It does not specify how much compression, frame rate, color quality, or bitrate is used.

Stadia can use more data than a typical 1080p YouTube video because:

- **Higher frame rate:** Stadia commonly streams at **60 fps**, while much YouTube content is 24–30 fps. Twice as many frames can mean substantially more data.
- **Games are difficult to compress:** Fast camera movement, detailed grass/foliage, particles, HUD elements, and constantly changing scenes give video compression less opportunity to reuse information from prior frames.
- **Low latency matters:** YouTube can buffer far ahead and use encoding strategies that prioritize squeezing the file size down. A cloud game needs to respond to your controller input almost immediately, so it uses real-time encoding settings that may be less bandwidth-efficient.
- **Quality targets differ:** Stadia needs text, UI, and rapid movement to remain readable/playable. Aggressive compression artifacts can be more disruptive in a game than in a passive video.
- **Codec/settings may differ:** YouTube often serves very efficient codecs such as VP9 or AV1, especially for popular videos, and dynamically lowers bitrate when appropriate. Stadia’s stream quality depends on the device, connection, codec support, and selected mode.

For example, Stadia’s 1080p/60 mode was often quoted around **10–12.6 GB per hour** (roughly 22–28 Mbps). A typical 1080p YouTube stream may be only around **3–6 GB per hour**, especially at 30 fps—though high-quality 1080p60 YouTube can use more.

So it is not that Stadia’s pixels are “more 1080p”; it is sending a more demanding, real-time 60-fps interactive video stream at a higher bitrate.

Think of 1080p as the size of a canvas: both images have 1,920 × 1,080 pixels. But one can be saved with much heavier compression than the other.

At the same 1080p resolution, differences can include:

- **Bitrate:** More bits per second preserves more image detail. Low bitrate causes blockiness, smearing, banding, and muddy motion.
- **Frame rate:** 1080p30 and 1080p60 are both 1080p, but 60 fps has twice as many images each second and smoother motion.
- **Compression codec:** H.264, VP9, AV1, etc. can produce different quality at the same bitrate.
- **Color quality:** Streams can differ in color depth, chroma subsampling, HDR support, and color range.
- **Motion/detail:** A static talking-head video can look excellent at a low bitrate; a fast-moving game needs far more data to look comparably clean.

So two things can both be “1080p” while one looks noticeably worse or better. Resolution tells you **how many pixels are displayed**, not how accurately each pixel’s color and detail survive compression.
